messages.author: 712283276713fe00
messages.subject: Basic assumption of gdistsamp?
parts:
Hello, this is a very basic question but hopefully it will seem refreshing/easy for someone to answer, rather than just annoying… :)

The definition of phi is the probability that something is “available for detection” or the probability that something is detectable if at zero distance from the point or line. For example, if a point count lasts 5 minutes but whales only spout once every 10 minutes, then phi = 0.5, and this could be used as a multiplier if known (2x in this case). In standard distance sampling, individuals could be moving around randomly between repeated point counts, as long as there are enough points to be representative of a larger study area for which you want to estimate density (and the point count locations could even move around randomly). However, for GDISTSAMP to correctly estimate phi, it requires that individuals have FIXED locations between repeated point counts, correct? (Complete closure with no movement in/out of any plots?)

For example, assume we are estimating density for a very non-cryptic bird species (phi = 1), and that the birds move around randomly between point counts. Using Figure 1 of Chandler et al. 2011 (25 point count plots, about 50 birds in the entire study area, and about 5 total birds within all plots at any one time, such that total plot area is about 1/10 the study area). With standard distance sampling, assuming each point count is a snapshot, we could repeat the points as many times as we like, and get a density estimate of 5 per total plot area, or 50 per study area. But with GDISTSAMP, we would be in trouble if there is random movement of the birds (or ANY movement) between repeated point counts, because phi would become underestimated and so we would overestimate density. Is this correct?

--Ed

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Basic assumption of gdistsamp?
parts:
hi Ed,
 I'm not so sure that this is a basic question at all.

 I think you're right, however.  The models in unmarked, by my understanding, apply to the "random temporary emigration" as opposed to "spatial temporary emigration" (individuals moving off plot).  I do think, however, that the random temporary emigration model approximates pretty well the spatial temporary emigration which I think is a point of the Chandler et al. (2011) paper.  [I guess I should feel more confident in saying that since I was a coauthor....].
 
 The way I think about it there are actually two levels of temporary emigration in many practical situations:

 1. First individuals draw a location (at each time) and some of them are inside the circle.
 2. Then they decide to become invisible or not.

 The individuals occur in the circle and are visible with probability phi.

 IF both things are happening then I don't think the corrected density estimates (as in Chandler et al. 2011) would be strictly unbiased, in general.  But if one or the other of the two things is not happening then things should be good (this is what Chandler et al. 2011 showed). 

 I would like to see a simulation study to address this.  i.e., simulate both things happening and see what the result is. I don't think we did that in the Chandler et al. 2011 paper.   [note: we discuss this a little bit in chapter 9 of the new AHM book but the discussion is brief and tentative because the issue hadn't occurred to me until writing that material].

 If people have something to add to this I'd like to hear about it.

regards
andy

messages.author: 403be63af7ebf220
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Basic assumption of gdistsamp?
parts:
Hi Ed,

I agree with what Andy said, but I want to attempt to clarify a few things. You asked:

"But with GDISTSAMP, we would be in trouble if there is random movement of the birds (or ANY movement) between repeated point counts, because phi would become underestimated and so we would overestimate density. Is this correct?"

This is not correct. As we showed in the paper, movement does not necessarily cause bias in the abundance/density estimator. One thing to keep in mind is that the appropriate abundance estimator depends on the context, and particularly the definition of availability. 

If availability is defined as the probability of being on the plot on occasion t (and demographic closure can be assumed), then abundance is estimated by: 

E(N(i,t)) = lambda(i)*phi(i,t)

where lambda(i) is the expected value of the superpopulation size M(i). In this case, abundance at site i changes over time due to movement (temporary emigration). In a spatially explicit setting, phi would be individual-specific, and thus this model is mis-specified. However, we demonstrated that, under a bivariate normal movement model, the estimator is unbiased.

Another common situation is one in which there isn't any movement, and phi is defined as the probability of being available for detection.  (Perhaps you do a short point count divided into several time intervals and birds are only available if they sing). In that case:

E(N(i,t)) = lambda(i)

and so abundance doesn't change over time, but availability does. 

Finally, the model could be used as a phenomenological description of population dynamics by letting phi be defined generally as the proportion of the superpopulation that is alive and on the plot at time t. Here again you would use E(N(i,t)) = M(i)*phi(i,t)). This might be a useful model in some situations, but I think it would be better to develop a function like pcountOpen for distance sampling data that includes a hidden Markov model to describe temporal dynamics. 

Richard
